mstts:express-as.prosody: Let’s talk about something we all wish we could avoid—grief. Most of us see it as this unpredictable, overwhelming landscape that’s just plain hard to navigate. But here’s the surprising thing: as the therapist and her clients discovered, grief sometimes opens doors we never even knew were there. For the therapist herself, losing a relationship felt like being hit by a tidal wave—sudden, disorienting, and relentless. She found herself cycling through anger, sadness, even numbness—all in the same day sometimes. There were days when she wondered if she’d ever feel whole again. But as she sat with her pain, something amazing started to happen. She began to notice tiny moments of beauty—a kind word from a friend, the peace of a quiet morning walk, or the comfort of a favorite song. These little things didn’t erase her grief, but they softened its sharpest edges. One of her clients, a father mourning his child, struggled to find any meaning in what he was going through. He carried so much guilt—about words left unsaid, about the ache that just wouldn’t go away. In therapy, he learned that grief isn’t something you just “get over.” Instead, it’s something you carry—with tenderness. He found comfort in little rituals—lighting a candle, writing letters, sharing memories with loved ones. Slowly, he realized that grief could actually exist alongside joy. Remembering didn’t have to mean being stuck in the past. Another client, facing the end of a long marriage, found herself grieving not just the relationship, but the future she’d always pictured. She was scared—scared of being alone, of starting over, of losing the person she thought she was. In therapy, she gave herself permission to mourn—not only the loss, but the dreams that wouldn’t come true. And in that honest space, she found the courage to imagine new possibilities, and to reconnect with parts of herself she’d forgotten. The therapist came to realize something truly powerful: for all its pain, grief can actually be a teacher. It shows us what really matters, strips away the masks, and invites us to be honest—with ourselves and with others. Grief reminds us that love and loss are two sides of the same coin. To grieve deeply? It means you’ve loved deeply, too.
